prompt: Some schools have replaced letter grades with written feedback only. Write an essay arguing whether this is a good idea.
text:
# Should Schools Drop Letter Grades for Written Feedback?

A letter grade is a small piece of information. A "B+" tells a student that their work was good but not great, and it says nothing about why. Some schools have decided that this trade is a bad one and now give only written feedback. I think they are mostly right. Written feedback teaches students more than grades do, but it works only if schools solve two practical problems: the time it takes teachers and the demands of college admissions.

## What grades do to learning

The strongest argument for written feedback is that students stop reading once they see a grade. Ruth Butler's 1988 study of schoolchildren found that students who received only comments improved on later tasks. Students who received a grade, or a grade with comments, did not improve as much. The grade drew their attention, and they used it to judge how they compared with classmates instead of how to improve.

That habit is the real cost of grading. When a grade decides a student's standing, the sensible goal is to get the grade, not to understand the material. Students ask what will be on the test, pick easy electives, avoid difficult problems and sometimes cheat. A student who fears a bad mark has little reason to attempt something hard and fail at it, yet that is how most people learn.

Written feedback changes what a student does with a returned assignment. A comment such as "Your argument is clear, but your second paragraph assumes what you are trying to prove" tells the student what to fix. A "B" tells them nothing they can act on.

## Why a letter is less precise than it looks

Grades seem objective, but they combine many different things. A "B" might mean strong ideas with weak spelling, or average work that was handed in on time every day. Two teachers can give the same assignment different grades, and two schools can mean different things by an "A." The single letter hides all of this, and readers trust it more than they should.

Written feedback can describe what a student can do and where they struggle. A parent reading "Maya explains her reasoning well in math but makes frequent arithmetic errors when she hurries" learns more than from a "B-" in the same subject.

## The costs

The first cost is teacher time. Writing a useful paragraph about each student's work takes far longer than assigning a letter. A high school teacher with 150 students cannot write detailed comments on every assignment. If schools adopt written feedback without reducing class sizes or workloads, comments will turn into vague, repeated phrases like "good effort, keep it up," which are worse than a grade because they look informative and are not.

The second cost is that outsiders still want a summary. Colleges, scholarship committees and employers read thousands of applications and need some way to compare them. Schools that drop grades often end up producing a summary anyway, or admissions officers guess from test scores, which may favor students who can afford test preparation. Without a clear summary, students from lesser-known schools could be harder to evaluate and so be disadvantaged.

The third cost is that feedback can be uneven. Some teachers write well and others do not. Comments can also carry bias in their tone, such as praising some students for effort and others for talent. A grade, for all its flaws, is at least short enough that these differences are less visible.

## What a good version looks like

These problems are real, but they are problems of how schools carry out the change, not reasons to keep grades. A good system would have several features:

- **Clear standards.** Teachers describe what students should be able to do, and feedback refers to those standards, so comments mean the same thing across classrooms.
- **Manageable workloads.** Teachers give detailed comments on a few key assignments and use quicker methods, such as conferences or checklists, for the rest.
- **A plain summary for outsiders.** The school gives colleges a short statement of each student's level in each subject, written by teachers and based on the same standards. Colleges that have worked with such schools have generally been able to read these.
- **Revision.** Students use the feedback to improve their work and resubmit it, which is the point of giving feedback in the first place.

## Conclusion

Letter grades are convenient, but they teach students to chase marks instead of understanding, and they say very little about what a student actually knows. Written feedback is better for learning, and the research I know of supports it. It is also harder to do well, and a school that adopts it carelessly will lose the benefits. Schools should move away from letter grades, but only if they commit the time, training and clear standards that make the comments worth reading.
